prompt: Which of these graphs are bipartite (2-colourable)? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Bipartite. Alternate colours around the cycle; because 6 is even, the last vertex's colour differs from the first.
Bipartite. Colour vertices by depth parity from a root. A tree has no cycles at all, so certainly no odd cycles.
Not bipartite. All three vertices are mutually adjacent, so they need 3 colours.
Bipartite by definition: its two sides of 3 vertices each are the two colour classes.
Not bipartite. Alternating colours around an odd cycle forces the last vertex to clash with the first.

workedExample:
A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd-length cycle.

```
C6     even cycle    yes
tree   no cycles     yes
K3     odd cycle 3   no
K3,3   sides given   yes
C5     odd cycle 5   no
```

Try colouring C₅ to see the failure:

```
v0 R, v1 B, v2 R, v3 B, v4 R
v4 is adjacent to v0: R-R clash
```

A BFS (breadth-first search) that colours vertices by distance parity detects this in O(n + m) time, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges.

prompt: Five courses A–E have exam conflicts (shared students) forming a ring: A–B, B–C, C–D, D–E and E–A. What is the minimum number of exam slots so that no student has two exams at once?

options.explanation: Two slots would make the conflict graph bipartite, but it's a 5-cycle, an odd cycle. Alternating slots round the ring clashes at E–A.
Correct. The conflict graph is a five-cycle and needs three colours. One valid assignment gives slot one to A and C, slot two to B and D, and slot three to E.
5 would work but isn't minimal. Non-adjacent courses (like A and C) can share a slot.
4 is more than needed. Odd cycles need exactly 3 colours, regardless of length.

workedExample: Alternating two slots round the five-course ring makes the final course clash with the first, so two do not suffice. Assign A and C to one slot, B and D to a second, and E to a third. Every conflict edge then joins different slots. A lower bound of three plus an exhibited three-slot assignment proves the minimum.

prompt: In the simplified register-colouring model, four mutually interfering live values form K₄ and only 3 interchangeable registers are available. What must change?

options.text: Nothing special; 3 registers suffice because the graph has only 4 vertices
options.explanation: K₄ needs four colours. Four vertices bound the chromatic number above by four, but do not make three sufficient.

options.text: Reorder instructions so the greedy colouring uses 3 colours
options.explanation: No vertex order helps: K₄ needs 4 colours whatever algorithm colours it. Only changing the graph (e.g. by spilling or splitting live ranges) can help.

options.text: Spill at least one variable to memory (or otherwise shorten live ranges)
options.explanation: With the fixed interference graph, three registers cannot hold all four values. Spill a value or transform the program/live ranges, for example by rematerializing a value when needed.

options.text: Use the four colour theorem to fit them in 3 registers
options.explanation: The four colour theorem guarantees 4 colours for *planar* graphs. It says nothing about fitting into 3.

workedExample: Four pairwise-interfering values require four different registers in the fixed graph. Changing the order of greedy colouring cannot remove those conflicts. With only three registers, the allocator must change the problem, for example by spilling or splitting live ranges. Real architectures also impose register-class and fixed-register constraints.

prompt: For finite simple undirected graphs, select all the statements that are true.

options.text: Whether a graph has an Euler circuit can be decided in linear time
options.explanation: Check that all edge-bearing vertices are connected and every degree is even, in time linear in the number of vertices plus edges. Isolated vertices need not be visited by the edge-covering Euler circuit.

options.text: Whether a graph has a Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete
options.explanation: True. It is one of Karp's original NP-complete problems, and no polynomial-time algorithm is known.

options.text: Every graph with an Euler circuit also has a Hamiltonian cycle
options.explanation: False. The bowtie (two triangles sharing a vertex) has all degrees even but any tour of all 5 vertices would revisit the shared vertex.

options.text: If a simple graph has at least 3 vertices and every degree is at least half the vertex count, it has a Hamiltonian cycle
options.explanation: True. This is Dirac's theorem. It is sufficient, not necessary: a plain cycle Cₙ has degree 2 everywhere and is Hamiltonian.

options.text: Greedy colouring always finds the chromatic number
options.explanation: False. Greedy uses at most one more colour than the maximum degree, but a poor vertex order can use more colours than necessary, even on bipartite graphs.

workedExample:
Separate the easy problems from the hard ones. In the table, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges and k the number of colours allowed.

```
Euler circuit    degree test  O(n+m)
Hamilton cycle   NP-complete
k-colouring      NP-complete (k>=3)
bipartite test   BFS          O(n+m)
```

The bowtie counterexample:

```
  1   3
  |\ /|
  | 0 |
  |/ \|
  2   4
edges 0-1,1-2,2-0,0-3,3-4,4-0
deg(0)=4, others 2
```

Euler circuit: 0-1-2-0-3-4-0. A Hamiltonian cycle would have to leave the {1, 2} triangle and enter the {3, 4} triangle through vertex 0 both times, visiting it twice.
